question_text: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of weight gain, generalized weakness, and irregular menstrual cycles for the past 16 months. She began having symptoms of insomnia and depression 10 months ago. More recently, she has been having difficulties rising from a chair. She has a 2-year history of hypertension. Current medications include citalopram and hydrochlorothiazide. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb). BMI is 36 kg/m2. Her pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 134/76 mm Hg. She appears tired and has a full, plethoric face and central obesity. Examination of the skin shows violaceous linear striations on her lower abdomen. Two midnight serum cortisol studies show measurements of 288 μg/L and 253 μg/L (N < 90); a 24-hour urinary cortisol measurement was 395 μg (N < 300). Upon follow-up laboratory examination, the patient's serum ACTH levels were also elevated at 136 pg/mL (N = 7–50). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

                    ### Question
                    A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of weight gain, generalized weakness, and irregular menstrual cycles for the past 16 months. She began having symptoms of insomnia and depression 10 months ago. More recently, she has been having difficulties rising from a chair. She has a 2-year history of hypertension. Current medications include citalopram and hydrochlorothiazide. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb). BMI is 36 kg/m2. Her pulse is 92/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 134/76 mm Hg. She appears tired and has a full, plethoric face and central obesity. Examination of the skin shows violaceous linear striations on her lower abdomen. Two midnight serum cortisol studies show measurements of 288 μg/L and 253 μg/L (N < 90); a 24-hour urinary cortisol measurement was 395 μg (N < 300). Upon follow-up laboratory examination, the patient's serum ACTH levels were also elevated at 136 pg/mL (N = 7–50). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

                    ### Options
                    opa. MRI of the head with contrast
opb. Measure ACTH levels in inferior petrosal sinuses
opc. High-dose dexamethasone suppression test
opd. CT scan of the abdomen with contrast
ope. Bilateral adrenalectomy

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with classic symptoms of Cushing's syndrome, including weight gain, hypertension, and characteristic skin changes, alongside elevated midnight serum cortisol and 24-hour urinary cortisol levels. The elevated serum ACTH indicates an ACTH-dependent cause, likely from a pituitary adenoma or ectopic source. The most appropriate next step in evaluation is to measure ACTH levels in the inferior petrosal sinuses, as this procedure is the gold standard for differentiating between pituitary and ectopic sources of ACTH. While MRI of the head can identify pituitary adenomas, inferior petrosal sinus sampling provides more definitive localization of the source of ACTH secretion. Therefore, the best option is to measure ACTH levels in inferior petrosal sinuses.
